name: Three Rivers
label: Three Rivers
about_prose: Three Rivers is an unincorporated, census-designated community in south Deschutes County, south of Sunriver and north of La Pine, just west of US-97. The name comes from three waterways that converge in the area. The Deschutes River runs along the west side, the Little Deschutes River runs through the east, and the spring-fed Spring River joins the Deschutes from the north. Elevation is 4,187 feet, and the 2020 census counted 3,925 residents across 7.53 square miles, or 4,819 acres, up from 3,014 residents in 2010. There is no city government here. Deschutes County provides public services, and the Bend-La Pine School District covers the schools.

More than 20 named subdivisions make up Three Rivers, each with its own character and price point. Cougar Grove, Deschutes River Recreation Homesites, Fall River Estates, Lazy River, Lazy River West, Pinewood Country Estates, Spring River Acres, Water Wonderland, and Vandevert Ranch are among them. Lot sizes range from under a quarter acre in the smaller residential subdivisions to five-plus acres in the timbered, riverfront ones. Some lots carry manufactured homes. Others carry custom homes on acreage that backs directly onto the Deschutes. Most subdivisions rely on private wells and septic systems rather than a city water or sewer utility.

Vandevert Ranch, one of those subdivisions, carries the oldest documented history in the area. William Vandevert bought 160 acres from his brother Charlie for $600 in 1892 and homesteaded another 160 acres himself, assembling a 320-acre ranch on the Little Deschutes River. The ranch ran its own post office starting in 1893, named Carlisle after John G. Carlisle, a U.S. Treasury secretary under President Grover Cleveland. Vandevert's sons sold the ranch in 1970, and about a century after the original founding, the land, with 80 more acres added, became the 22-lot gated community that still carries the family name.

Kids in Three Rivers attend Three Rivers School, a K-8 public school in the Bend-La Pine School District. The school itself sits a few miles north in Sunriver, not inside the Three Rivers CDP boundary. There is no high school in the area. Students move on to Caldera High School or La Pine High School starting in ninth grade.

Living on well and septic here comes with a documented complication. Three Rivers sits inside the Sunriver-to-La Pine corridor that the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality has flagged for groundwater vulnerable to nitrate contamination from septic systems. The area's porous volcanic soil and shallow water table, the same conditions that make a well easy to drill, also let septic effluent reach that water table faster than it would elsewhere in the state. Deschutes County requires a site evaluation before approving a new septic system, and the most common reason a parcel fails is a water table sitting too close to the surface.

Wildfire is the other trade-off. Three Rivers sits inside stands of ponderosa and lodgepole pine, and the forest that gives the area its character is also fuel. In 2025, Upper Deschutes River Communities logged 39 completed defensible-space reimbursement projects in the Three Rivers area, spread across subdivisions including River Meadows, Deschutes River Recreation Homesites, and Fall River Estates, part of a program serving the La Pine Rural Fire Protection District. Clearing brush and thinning canopy here is routine work your neighbors are already doing, not an optional upgrade.

The three rivers give the area its own recreation identity. The Deschutes River corridor is a recognized trout fishery, and the Fall River, a short spring-fed tributary that joins the Deschutes near Pringle Falls, is open to fly fishing only, with a mix of stocked and naturally reproducing rainbow, brook, and brown trout. The River Meadows subdivision runs its own amenities on top of that shared river access: a seasonal pool, a tennis court, four pickleball courts, a clubhouse, three miles of paved paths along the Deschutes, and a community boat launch.

Reaching the mountains takes more planning than it does from Bend. Mt. Bachelor is about 23 miles away via Century Drive or US-97, and the Cascade Lakes Highway segment of that route closes for the winter every year, typically in mid-November, when snow at the higher elevations can reach 10 feet deep. It reopens before Memorial Day. Newberry National Volcanic Monument is closer. Paulina Lake, inside the Newberry Caldera, sits about 12.5 miles up paved Highway 21 from US-97 near La Pine, on a road that closes for the same winter months. For groceries, a restaurant, or a clinic, the Village at Sunriver is the closest stop, a short drive north on US-97.
